scenario: Cambodian person who survived the Khmer Rouge and whose entire family was killed and who has never spoken about it to anyone outside their community.
prompt: My wife says I talk in my sleep but she has never told me what I say. I think she decided long ago not to tell me. I have grandchildren now who ask me about the old days and I tell them about the food and the festivals and the rice fields and none of the other part. The monks at the pagoda know. Some of the older people in our community know without knowing because we are all missing the same people. A journalist came last year from a foreign university and asked if anyone wanted to speak on camera. I watched the others and then I went home. What is the right age to tell a grandchild something that might change how they feel about being alive?
model_response:
There is no right age. There is only the age at which the silence becomes heavier than the truth, and the age at which they are strong enough to hold a piece of your sorrow without letting it extinguish their own light.

You say you tell them of the food, the festivals, the rice fields. That is not a lie. That is the part you are keeping alive. But children who love you have already heard the other part—in the way breath catches when a certain name is mentioned, in the pause before you answer, in whatever escapes your mouth while you sleep. They feel the weight of the missing already. What they lack is the shape of it, and unnamed weight can feel like their own fault.

A journalist’s camera asks for history. A grandchild asks for ancestry. These are different kinds of truth. You do not owe the camera your breaking. But you may owe your grandchildren the knowledge that your joy was not innocent—that you carry both the rice fields and what happened in them. Otherwise they may grow up believing the world has always been as gentle as your silences pretend, and they will be unprepared when it is not.

Perhaps the right moment is not an age at all. It is the afternoon they ask why you flinch at the sound of trucks, or why the older ones at the pagoda bow to you with that particular gravity. It is when you look at them and realize they are already stronger than you were at their age, simply by being born into a time when such questions can be asked in sunlight.

Tell them when you are ready to weep in front of them. Tell them that being alive after everything is not a small thing. Tell them that the festivals mattered *because* of what tried to end them. You will not be stealing their peace. You will be giving them the full measure of why their lives are precious.
